header.title: Mannahatta along the Hudson
header.subtitle: Tracing today’s landmarks back to their ecological roots; and what that means for restoration going forward.

data.content: Towering buildings. Sprawling neighborhoods. Endless concrete. 1.6 million people packed onto one island, swelling to nearly 3.9 million on an average workday. This is the New York most of us know; a place that can feel entirely apart from nature. But it wasn’t always this way.

On the afternoon of September 12, 1609, Henry Hudson sailed into a deep harbor suitable for trade, and a defensible collection of islands at the mouth of a tidal estuary, where a freshwater river met the saltwater of the Atlantic — ocean giving way to sandy beach, beach to forest, forest to freshwater wetland. 

In Manhattan alone, there were as many as 1,195 plant species and 658 species of fish, reptiles, amphibians, birds, and mammals, within 55 distinct ecological communities, across a landscape of 500 hills, 88 miles of streams, 21 ponds, and 300 springs.

The Lenape had known this place for 8,000 to 10,000 years before Hudson arrived. They fished heavily each spring, hunted and gathered through the summer, and grew corn, beans, and squash in fields before packing up each fall.

steps.title: Where we are now: Pier 57
steps.body: You're standing at Pier 57 right now. Look around – almost everything along this stretch of shoreline and the surrounding area has a hidden history beneath it.

steps.title: Gansevoort Beach, Little Island, Chelsea Piers
steps.body: Many landmarks amongst Hudson River Park, from Pier 57 and Gansevoort Beach to Little Island and Chelsea Piers, were all built on landfill, over what was once the Marine Deepwater.

steps.title: The Whitney
steps.body: Head inland and you'd have hit the beach. From the Battery up to 42nd Street, the Hudson shore was a nearly continuous stretch of sand, a mosaic of Maritime Beach and Salt Shrub communities held the line between water and land. This is roughly where The Whitney stands today.

steps.title: The High Line
steps.body:
The Whitney marks the site of Sapokanikan, a Lenape settlement, canoe landing, trading site, and launching point for travel west, across the river on the Mid-Mahicanituk Crossing to Hobocanhackingh settlement on Jersey shore's Hoboken.

The south end of the High Line roughly follows the Sapokanikan Path, which ran north along the Maritime Beach and Salt Shrub shoreline.

pins.label: The southern entrance of the High Line

steps.title: Chelsea Market
steps.body: East along the trail, inland from the shore, stood forest, the kind of mixed hardwood now known as Appalachian Oak Hickory and Oak-Tulip Tree forest, where Chelsea Market stands today.

steps.title: Madison Square Garden
steps.body: Further northeast and further inland — what's now the Target on West 23rd Street to Madison Square Garden — was wetland, a 42-acre mosaic of Appalachian Oak-Pine Forest, Shallow Emergent Marsh, and Shrub Swamp known as the 7th Ave. Wetland.

steps.title: The Vessel
steps.body: A bit further north along the coast lay Clapboard Meadow, a 27-acre tidal salt marsh — Low Salt Marsh at the water's edge, High Salt Marsh further inland — where Hudson Yards, The Shed, and The Vessel stand today.

data.content:
We assembled this landscape of Mannahatta from four centuries of evidence: historical maps, art and literature, written descriptions, herbarium and museum specimens, archaeological artifacts, species field guides, and scientific evidence such as pollen layered in pond mud, the width of old tree rings, and the chemistry of rock and soil.

From that evidence, we reconstruct the past by layering everything onto the geography of the city today: the hills, streams, and shoreline; the soil and bedrock beneath them and where people most likely lived. Put together, this becomes a set of maps and an all-encompassing computer-rendered view of Manhattan's land and water as they stood just before European contact.

The process starts with the maps themselves: compile historical maps, digitize them, and georeference them. In other words, line up their landmarks with the modern street grid so they occupy the same coordinate system. From each map, we pull out anything ecological it recorded, such as a stream, a hill, or a marsh. We then stacked those findings into a single synthesized picture: hydrology, soil, bedrock, shoreline, groundwater, geology, and known Lenape sites. From this combined layer, we model where individual species most likely lived.

Made by British military cartographers during the wartime occupation of New York City in 1782–83, this 10-foot-long survey was meant to help loyalist forces plan Manhattan's defense and prepare for an attack by the Continental Army. To do that job well, it had to record everything on the island — not just roads, fortifications, and farms, but the hills, streams, beaches, marshes, and wetlands beneath them.

That's what makes it the single most valuable source for reconstructing this landscape's ecology. It shows elevation, glacial hills, slope, shoreline, and wetlands in enough detail that roughly 200 separate ecological features were pulled and georeferenced from this one map alone. It was drawn about 170 years after Henry Hudson's arrival, so we work from an assumption: if a hill, stream, or marsh still existed in 1782, it very likely existed in 1609 too.

data.text: Merrill 1902, NYC Folio of the Geologic Atlas NY-Paterson Quadrangle Surficial Geology

data.content: In 1902, state geologist Frederick Merrill compiled geological surveys of the bedrock, topography, and surficial geology of New York’s five boroughs. This was the first detailed map of the city's surficial geology: a mosaic of four quadrangles covering the New York City region, georeferenced and stitched together into one. The map shows the sand, gravel, and clay that made up the surficial baseline, which controls the soil development, hydrology and nutrient availability that dictates plant and animal distributions. This information is an essential used to inform land use management decisions.

data.text: Colton & Co 1836, Topographical Map Of The City and County Of New-York

data.content: Made by J.H. Colton, a prominent 19th-century map and atlas publisher, this 1836 survey is a detailed topographical map of Manhattan and its surroundings, produced for civic planning as the city's street grid was actively expanding. It catches the island mid-transformation: downtown is already gridded and built up, while the land further north, with real elevation still visible, remains largely forested. It's a snapshot of the landscape just before infrastructure caught up with it, taken at the exact moment you can still see it wants to be a forest.

data.text: Viele 1865, Sanitary & Topographical Map of the City and Island of New York, 1865

data.content:
Made by civil engineer and former U.S. representative Egbert L. Viele, this map earned the nickname "the water map" for its purpose: tracking the streams that were rapidly being filled in and culverted across the city. Viele had a public health argument to make as he believed paving over the city's natural drainage created a "humid miasmatic" atmosphere that spread disease, including yellow fever.

To make that case, he documented what was disappearing: the canals, hills, swamps, rivers, ponds, meadows, drainage basins, and the original shoreline of Manhattan before landfill expanded the island. That documentation had a long afterlife: contractors and architects still consult Viele's map today to avoid building over old, buried waterways.

Made in 1891 by J.R. Bien and C.C. Vermeule from original surveys of the New York–New Jersey border region, this atlas was built to give planners accurate physical and economic data ahead of the 1898 consolidation of New York's five boroughs with contour lines, elevation, topography, streets, railroads, and ferry routes across the whole metropolitan area.

It's most valuable as a document of the shoreline changing in real time: active wharves and ferry paths, docks lining the coast, and the visible edge of landfill pushing the water back as the street grid extends over what used to be marsh and open water.

Much of what we know about Lenape settlement in this area comes from R.P. Bolton, a British-born civil engineer, historian, and archaeologist who spent decades mapping and excavating Native American sites across New York City, and published his findings in, “New York City in Indian Possession” and “Indian Paths to the Great Metropolis.”

data.content: With this information, we built a computer model of where Lenape settlement was most likely: seeded with the actual locations of known artifacts, then refined using factors like distance to fresh water, distance to shore, and shelter from winter winds.

The species list draws on field guides and naturalist accounts going back centuries, compiled within a 75-mile radius of Columbus Circle (and out to a thousand yards from today's shoreline for marine species). In total: 35 references for plants, including 8 full book-length treatments, 22 for birds, and 20 for mammals. Among the references is John Torrey's 1818, “Catalogue of Plants Growing Wild Within 30 Miles of the City.”

A species made the list only if it passed three tests: it couldn't be an import from elsewhere in the world, it couldn't have expanded into the region within the last 400 years, and it had to have a real habitat relationship with one of Mannahatta's ecological communities. Species that passed were then matched to their known habitat needs — soil type, distance to water, slope, ecosystem type — and projected onto the landscape layers already built from the maps.

items.caption: The title page of John Torrey’s Calendarium Florae for the Vicinity of New York.
The title page of John Torrey's Catalogue of Plants within Thirty Miles of the City of New York.

data.content:
Those relationships are what became the “Muir Web,” named for the naturalist John Muir, who wrote that everything is "bound fast by a thousand invisible cords that cannot be broken, to everything in the universe." Rather than plotting species in isolation, the Muir Web maps what each one depends on — food, water, shelter, and the other species and habitat elements around it — then layers those relationships across the island to predict where any given plant or animal most likely lived.

It's not an exact record, but it's a methodical reconstruction. Species move, and ranges shift as habitat and climate change, so any reconstruction like this carries real uncertainty… this is how we got as many as 1,195 plant species and 658 species of fish, reptiles, amphibians, birds, and mammals, sorted into 55 ecological communities.

At NYBG’s Urban Conservation Program, we are not only interested in understanding NYC’s historical ecology, but we are also thinking about how the current natural areas and built environment are connected to this history, and what that means for the future of nature in the city. 

The more a steward knows about a site's history, the better-informed its future can be. Planting native species, those that occur naturally in the region today, is a restoration staple – rebuilding food webs shaped by millennia of co-evolution between plants, pollinators, and wildlife. 

The High Line puts this urban ecology into practice, with more than 600 species of plants,  of which 55% are native. By biomass, over 70% of the park's plantings are native.

data.quote: “The original design intent of the park was to use ecological habitats – woodlands, woodland edge, grasslands and wetlands – as a framework.”
data.attribution: Richard Hayden, Senior Director of Horticulture at the High Line

data.content:
The High Line gardens have also been found to support 33 species of bees with many migrating birds and bats finding food, shelter and nesting sites on the High Line. And a recent study with Climate Central found the High Line's trees and plantings made the park on average over 7 degrees cooler than the surrounding neighborhood.

That said, ecosystems aren't fixed, and local conditions have changed too drastically for the past to serve as the sole blueprint. A century of development filled in wetlands and shorelines, cleared forests, and buried streams; new species arrived through horticulture; and climate change has brought rising temperatures, more frequent flooding, and new pests and pathogens. Together, these disturbances alter the conditions for growth: the soil, hydrology, topography, and relationships between species.

Ecologists call the result a novel ecosystem. Because conditions have changed so much, most of these systems can't be restored to their historical state; the goal instead is a system that works under today's conditions and tomorrow's. Practitioners increasingly think in terms of function, not just species – the food webs, pollination, and other relationships that keep a system running – and how to preserve those even as the species that carry them out change.

data.caption: A restoration practitioner tends to native plantings along The High Line.

data.content:
Restoration practitioners today still lean on native and pollinator-friendly planting as the foundation, increasingly paired with an eye toward climate and urban stress resiliency: plants able to withstand or mitigate drought and heavy stormwater, the added heat radiating off concrete and pavement, deep shade cast by buildings, tight or isolated planting spaces, and pollution.

Some practitioners are also rethinking how to manage invasive species already established here, weighing which to remove against which now serve a real function in a changed system. Others go further still, experimenting with assisted migration and assisted gene flow: deliberately introducing plants from populations further south that are already adapted to warmer conditions.

A short walk from Pier 57, Hudson River Park's Gansevoort Peninsula shows this work underway: in 2022, the Park Trust installed salt marsh plantings and nearly 300 reef balls and gabions in the river to rebuild oyster habitat, improve water quality, and strengthen shoreline resilience. While centuries of altering this shoreline can't be undone, Gansevoort shows that the function it once served can still be rebuilt.
